To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Acute murine Aia is not affected by the disruption of osteoblast glucocorticoid signaling.
Acute murine Aia is not affected by disrupted osteoblastic glucorticoid signalling.
osteoblast glucocorticoid (GC) signalling does not affect antigen-induced arthritis (a model of rheumatoid arthrits) in mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the study of the effect of the immune system on the immune system.
the development and application of new materials, processes, and devices to address problems of energy efficiency, environmental impact, and sustainability.
the role of osteoblasts in the initiation and progression of arthritis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
osteoblastic GCs do not play a significant role in the pathogenesis of AIA.
GC signalling in osteocytes is not involved in the initiation and/or progression of acute AIA.
the osteoblastic GC pathway is not involved in the initiation and/or maintenance of acute AIA in tg mice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
osteoblast-derived GCs do not play a role in the pathogenesis of RA.
osteoblast-derived glucocorticoids do not contribute to the initiation or maintenance of arthritis in either a K/BxN or AIA model.
osteoblastic GC-signal is important in K/BxN arthritis but not in antigen-induced arthritis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the osteoblast is not an important player in the pathogenesis of AIA.
osteoblast-derived GCs are not involved in the modulation of T cell-mediated inflammatory responses.
osteoblast glucocorticoid receptor signalling plays a key role in the development of K/Bx N serum-induced arthritis but not in the T cell-mediated model of antigen-induced murine arthritis.
